reasonToGo: The road west out of the junction ends at the village here, and so does the water: this is one of three surveyed regions on Thirstwold with a spring on it, and all seven desert springs the world has charted are on this landmass. Parties work the seam where the river ground runs out into the sand — water off the two crossings, and whatever the dune front has finished with.

hazards.name: The bed that moves
hazards.description: The channel here runs in a dozen shallow threads across a wide gravel bed, and which of the threads is the deep one is a different answer between one crossing and the next. A cart taken over on last season's line goes in to the axle and stays there.

hazards.name: The front comes down
hazards.description: The dune ranks on the dry side of the region walk toward the river a little every year, and everything a party leaves on that side — a cairn, a stake, a wheel rut, a cache — is gone inside a season. A route walked out cannot be walked back by memory.
hazards.note: Absence hazard: the harm is the mark that no longer exists. Nothing in the runtime enum expresses ground that forgets.

resources.name: Front salvage
resources.description: Iron, glass and worked leather off what the sand covered before this village stood and has now uncovered again, gathered in the weeks between the front exposing a thing and the front taking it back.

resources.name: Ford water
resources.description: Drawn above both crossings and never below them, in the skins the village keeps standing at each bank. Water filled below a ford comes up with the bed in it, and the whole of Thirstwold prices everything else against a skin of it.

landmarks.name: Glasswold Barchan
landmarks.description: Seven and a half kilometres of sand ridges set square across the wind, rank behind rank like a swell that stopped. It is the near edge of the sand and it is moving; the far edge of it is not on any sheet.

landmarks.name: Confluence beyond Dunespar
landmarks.description: The dry tongue of ground between two channels just above where they join — under a kilometre across, and the piece of the road-head the village puts its stores on, because the floods take the bank on either side of it and leave the bench standing.
